tracks.title: The run that outlives the request
tracks.text: Lesson 05 point 4 — spawning. A sub-lesson, under agents. [curious] Here's the question this one answers. Every agent demo you've ever seen dies with its HTTP request. You ask for something that takes ten minutes… and request-and-response has no answer for you. The parent lesson — agents — sold the idea of a worker hired for the long run. This page is the unglamorous machinery underneath that promise. What process, exactly, is the agent… and who keeps it alive after you hang up the phone. The whole lesson fits in one line. The caller is disposable. The run is not.

tracks.title: The run that outlives the request
tracks.text: First — the run that outlives the request. Picture the failure. You ask for ten minutes of work, and the request model breaks three ways. First… the connection times out, somewhere around thirty seconds. Second… you hold the socket open and pray the proxy, the load balancer, and the laptop lid all cooperate for ten straight minutes. [sighs] They don't. Third… you give up and build the escape hatch everyone builds — a job queue, a worker pool, a status table, a websocket relay. You rebuild Sidekiq around every single agent. The same plumbing… every project… just to answer one question. Did it finish yet.

tracks.title: Spawning, defined
tracks.text: The definition. Spawning is starting a run as a supervised, named process. One call returns an id… in milliseconds. The run then works for minutes, under a supervisor, addressable by that id from anywhere — including from itself. And here's what matters. None of this is a job framework bolted on. The supervisor… the named registry… the process-per-run — these are the BEAM's own primitives. The same ones that have run phone networks for thirty years. An agent run is not a row in a queue table. It's a process… with a supervisor watching it.

tracks.title: One call, an id, a 202
tracks.text: [curious] One call, an id, and a 202. You start a run with a single HTTP call. POST to slash api slash run. You hand it a body — a system prompt, a task, a step budget. And it returns before the run does any work at all. Listen to what comes back. id… run-1742. status… running. And the status code is 202 — accepted, working on it. Not done. The instant your caller has that id, it is free to walk away. Now, the id itself — it's run, dash, an integer. Not a long random UUID. A simple counter. Three knobs ride in that body. First… max steps, the ceiling on the loop. At this door the default is forty. Second… model, which model drives the loop. And third — and this is the interesting one — exec. Exec isn't really a parameter. It's a trust grant. It unlocks host-brokered tools — git, publish, image, working directory access. Never raw bash… that hatch was deleted on purpose. And it's only honored when the engine explicitly allows it. Ask without the grant… and you simply don't get those tools. One last thing. The command-line tool — wbx agent run — is the very same call wearing a friendlier face. There is no second code path.

tracks.title: The receptionist and the worker
tracks.text: Now the load-bearing trick — the receptionist and the worker. A run is not one process. It's two. And the split is what makes everything else easy. Picture the supervision tree as a story. At the top sits the application supervisor. Hanging off it, two permanent children — a registry that maps id to process… and a dynamic supervisor that spawns the runs. Under that supervisor, one session per run — run-1742, run-1743 — each registered by its id. Think of each session as a receptionist. Its entire job is to stay responsive. It answers… what's your status. Subscribe me. Here's a human review. Instantly… always… because it never does the slow work itself. So where does the slow work go? To a second process — unnamed — that hangs off the session by a dotted line. When the session boots, it spawns this worker, and the worker grinds through the model-and-tools loop for however many minutes it takes. The receptionist holds a handle to it… and keeps answering the phone. [excited] That's the whole magic. When you poll for status, you're talking to the receptionist, not the worker. The worker could be ten seconds deep in a slow tool call… and your status answer still returns instantly. And one more thing the tree teaches — those two children, the registry and the supervisor, are permanent. They're up and waiting before any HTTP listener accepts a single connection. The machinery exists before the door opens.

tracks.title: Every step, three sinks
tracks.text: Next — every step, three sinks. Each time the loop calls a tool, it produces one step event. One shape, the same one the whole engine speaks — the step number, the agent, the tool, its arguments, the output, an exit code, an error, a duration, and a timestamp. And that single event fans out to three places. Picture the three as a table, and here's its verdict. The first sink is the websocket — live fanout to every watcher, sliced to five hundred characters a frame, and it dies the moment the socket closes. The second sink is a file called underscore steps dot jsonl — the append-only ledger, two hundred characters a line, and it survives everything because it's a file on disk. The third is events dot org — the readable transcript, three hundred characters a step, rendered when the run finishes, and it survives only if the run was given a durable place to live. The middle one is the one that matters most. That ledger is written on every step… regardless of any caller. So nothing escapes by construction. You can ignore the websocket entirely… and the trail still exists. [curious] And one guard lives right here. Every tool call is bounded at a hundred and fifty seconds. A tool that wedges gets shut down and becomes a tool error the model sees. Never a stalled run.

tracks.title: Poll or stream
tracks.text: Now — poll, or stream. Because the receptionist was keeping every step all along, watching a run is just a lookup. Two ways. First… poll. A GET to slash api slash run slash the id. Mid-run, you get back status running, steps seven, and a live list. Minutes later, you get status done, steps twelve, the result, the list of tools it used — shell, fetch, vfs write, done — and the whole transcript inline. One honest quirk to script around. An unknown id here returns a 200, with an error body that says no such run. Not a 404. Check the body… not just the code. Second… stream. A websocket upgrade, with a ten-minute idle timeout. Picture the frames as they arrive. First frame — subscribed, with the id. Then a frame per step — step zero, tool shell, some output. Step one, tool fetch, output… fetch failed, HTTP 404. And finally — done, result… three dead links found, report written. Those outputs are sliced to five hundred characters a frame — enough to watch the run think, not the whole payload. So the rule of thumb. A script that wants the final answer… polls. A UI that wants to show the run thinking… streams. Same data. Two doors.

tracks.title: The run that knows its name
tracks.text: Here's the move that turns spawning into a building block — the run that knows its own name. When the runtime spawns a run, it injects one thing into the agent's environment. WB underscore RUN… equals the run id. The run knows its own name. That sounds small until you see what it unlocks. A run can build a URL that routes back into its own mailbox. It can hand a human a place to send a decision… then block… and wait until that decision arrives. The review lands, gets pushed live to watchers, queued in order, and even written to a file so the record survives the process. This is the primitive underneath human-in-the-loop — and that has its own deep dive. For now, just hold the seam… a run that can address itself.

tracks.title: The other spawner, born at boot
tracks.text: [curious] Now the other spawner — born at boot. Everything so far was runs born on demand. One POST, one process. But there's a second spawner with the same engine inside. Standing agents are born at boot, from a declared manifest, under a static supervisor. You write them in a small org file. Picture it. A title — crew. Then a heading… wren… with properties pointing at a definition, a lifecycle, and an interval of ten minutes. Then a second heading… moss… pointing at an editor definition, and nothing else. Point an environment variable at that file and the supervisor starts one worker per heading. Walk the math the manifest implies. Wren first ticks at boot-grace plus zero. Moss starts staggered — thirty seconds later by default — so two agents don't slam the engine in the same instant. Wren runs every ten minutes. Moss declared no interval… so it defaults to once an hour. Both runs queue on a global gate that caps concurrency at two — a worker grabs a slot before its run and releases it afterward, so a wedged run can't starve its peers. Each run is killed at fifteen minutes of wall clock. And the cadence survives restarts — a small file under the data directory means a reboot doesn't reset the clock. Now compare the two spawners as a table, and here's the verdict. Ad-hoc runs come from the dynamic supervisor, on demand, unbounded. Standing agents come from a static supervisor, at boot, staggered, gated at two. Different doors… different budgets. But the last row is the punchline. [excited] The interior is the same Agent run loop, either way. The standing agent reaches the exact same loop your curl did. Two front doors… one engine.

tracks.title: Bounded at every layer
tracks.text: Bounded at every layer. A run could hang in a dozen places — a tool that never returns, a loop that never converges, a socket nobody closes. The design's answer is a ladder of time bounds. Picture the ladder, rung by rung. First rung… the tool call, a hundred and fifty seconds, enforced by the loop — a hang becomes a tool error the model sees. Second… the loop length, the step budget — a hang becomes a clean finish, not an infinite loop. Third… the keeper tick, fifteen minutes, enforced by the standing worker — a hang becomes a killed task, and its peers go free. Fourth… the websocket idle, ten minutes — a hang becomes a closed connection, the run untouched. And fifth… the no-work backoff, climbing to a thirty-minute cap — an idle agent stops burning calls. Read the verdict of that whole ladder in one line. Every bound turns a stall into a fact something else can handle. A wedged tool doesn't stall the run… it becomes an error the model routes around. An idle socket doesn't hold the run hostage… it just closes. These aren't safety nets bolted on after the fact. They're the shape of the thing.

tracks.title: What dies, what survives
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what dies, and what survives. Four limits, stated plainly, because they decide how you build on this. First… by default, a run leaves nothing behind. The spawned loop opens its own storage… and the default is in-memory. The promise of a resumable, replicable run is true only when you hand it a durable path. No path… no residue. Second… an engine restart kills every in-flight run. Sessions are supervised children, not saved across a restart. What survives is exactly three files — the steps ledger, the per-run review log, and the transcript, if the storage was on disk. Third… a hard-crashed worker leaves a zombie. The worker is a plain spawn — unlinked, unmonitored. If it crashes outright, the session never hears the done message… and shows status running, forever. [sighs] We found no sweeper that reaps these. So treat a run stuck on running, past your budget, as suspect — not as still working. And fourth… a session crash re-runs, it does not resume. If the session itself crashes, the supervisor restarts it with the same id and task… and runs the whole thing again, from step zero. History lost. None of this is hidden. Build on what's durable… don't assume the live process is.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Does the run survive my laptop closing? Yes — if the engine is somewhere else. The caller is disposable by design. Reconnect later and poll the id. If the engine is your laptop, then no — closing it stops the engine. Can I cancel a run? Honestly… we found no kill endpoint here. The brakes are the step budget and the time bounds. If you need a hard cancel, verify the current API before relying on one. How many runs at once? Ad-hoc runs are unbounded by design — each one is its own supervised process. Standing agents are capped at two by the gate, on purpose. Why did my run say running forever? Almost certainly the zombie case — the unlinked worker crashed hard, so the session never got its done message. And… is this a job queue under the hood? [chuckles] No. No queue table, no worker pool you provision, no relay you stand up. It's a supervised process per run, named in a registry, on the BEAM. The thing that runs phone networks… runs your agent.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's spawning. One supervised process per run… named by id… started with a call that returns in milliseconds. A receptionist that always answers… and a worker that does the minutes of work. The caller dies… the run doesn't care. [curious] From here, the way is clear. Up to the parent — agents — for what a run is actually for. Inward to loops, for what happens inside the spawned process. Or outward to orchestration, for who calls spawn on a cadence. But the one thing to carry away is this. The run outlives the request… because the run was never the request. It was a process… with a supervisor… waiting to outlast you.
